hero.title: The Technology Behind the Work
hero.subtitle: Vue, TypeScript, .NET and Azure, built to WCAG 2.2 Level AA accessibility, UK GDPR compliance and Google's Core Web Vitals thresholds. These are the standards every project is held to.

foundations.heading: The Foundations
foundations.subtitle: Strong fundamentals for reliable, accessible software.

html.title: Semantic HTML
html.description: Every site is built from semantic HTML5 elements, with proper landmark roles (<header>, <nav>, <main>, <footer>, <article>, <section>). That gives the page a logical document structure: something search engines can read and assistive technologies can move through efficiently. SEO and accessibility both benefit from the same work.

css.title: Modern CSS
css.description: CSS Grid and Flexbox for responsive layouts, container queries for component-level responsiveness, and custom properties (design tokens) for theming that stays maintainable. Leaving out heavy CSS frameworks means smaller bundles and faster page loads.

typescript.title: JavaScript & TypeScript
typescript.description: TypeScript adds type safety to JavaScript, catching bugs at compile time instead of in the browser. Typed interfaces define the data contracts and make refactoring safe, so fewer errors reach production and whoever maintains the code next gets up to speed faster.

frameworks.heading: Frameworks and Tooling
frameworks.subtitle: Vue 3, Nuxt, and Vite for high-performance modern applications.

vue.title: Vue 3
vue.description: Vue 3 is a JavaScript framework for building user interfaces. The Composition API makes logic reusable and testable and works well with TypeScript. Its reactivity system is efficient and predictable, and single-file components keep template, logic and styles together. With a small bundle size, Vue suits marketing sites and complex applications equally well.
vue.f1: Composition API for reusable, testable logic
vue.f2: Reactive data binding and computed properties
vue.f6: Virtual DOM with optimised patch algorithm

nuxt.title: Nuxt
nuxt.description: Nuxt is a meta-framework built on Vue 3, providing server-side rendering (SSR), static site generation (SSG) and hybrid rendering modes. SSR hands fully-rendered HTML to search engines and users on the first request, which helps SEO and perceived performance. SSG pre-renders pages at build time, so they can be served at maximum speed from an edge cache. File-based routing cuts out the boilerplate and makes the codebase easier to work in.
nuxt.f1: Server-side rendering (SSR) for SEO and performance
nuxt.f2: Static site generation (SSG) for edge-cached sites
nuxt.f4: File-based routing with automatic code splitting
nuxt.f5: Built-in SEO and meta tag management

vite.title: Vite & the Build Pipeline
vite.description: Vite is a build tool that uses native ES modules, so the dev server starts instantly and hot module replacement (HMR) is near-immediate. Production builds run through Rollup: optimised bundles with code splitting, tree shaking to strip out dead code, and automatic vendor chunk splitting. Development gets quicker and the bundles you ship get smaller.
vite.f1: Instant server start with native ESM
vite.f4: Automatic code splitting and tree shaking

apis.heading: APIs and Integrations
apis.subtitle: Secure, versioned, and well-documented API design.
apis.p1: Many applications need a backend API to handle data, authentication, payments and third-party integrations. I design and build REST and GraphQL APIs with OpenAPI contracts, semantic versioning and documentation. REST endpoints follow standard HTTP status codes (200 OK, 201 Created, 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 404 Not Found, 500 Internal Server Error) and use HTTP verbs (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) consistently.
apis.p2: Authentication uses established protocols: OAuth 2.0 for delegated access and JWT (JSON Web Tokens) for stateless session management. Rate limiting protects APIs from abuse, and CORS policies are configured correctly for cross-origin requests. Backend services are built in .NET (C#) or Node.js depending on what the project needs, both strongly typed and both with mature frameworks behind them.
apis.p3: Data persistence uses relational databases (SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL) with normalised schema design, appropriate indexing, and transactional integrity. Third-party integrations include payment gateways (Stripe, PayPal), booking systems (Booksy, Square), CRM platforms (HubSpot, Zoho), and email services (Mailchimp, SendGrid). Each integration is abstracted behind a clean interface so dependencies can be swapped without rewriting application logic.
apis.p4: REST and GraphQL solve the same problem in different ways. REST gives you one URL per resource and is simpler to cache, debug and document, which makes it the right default for most business websites and integrations. GraphQL gives the client a single endpoint and lets it request exactly the fields it needs. That helps when one screen pulls from many sources or mobile bandwidth is limited, at the cost of more complex caching and a steeper learning curve. For a small business site with a contact form and a booking integration, REST is almost always the better choice.

accessibility.heading: Accessibility Built In From the Start
accessibility.subtitle: WCAG 2.2 compliance for inclusive, usable web experiences.
accessibility.p1: Every site I build targets WCAG 2.2 Level AA. It is the standard referenced by UK accessibility obligations and the level most commercial and public sector contracts ask for, covering keyboard operability, screen reader support, colour contrast and error handling. Accessibility is designed in from the first decision, because retrofitting it before launch is where the cost lands. WAI-ARIA attributes (aria-label, aria-labelledby, aria-describedby, aria-live, role) are used sparingly, to add meaning where HTML alone falls short.
accessibility.p2: Keyboard use is tested on every build: each interactive element has a visible focus indicator, focus order follows reading order, and there are no keyboard traps. Screen reader testing uses NVDA (Windows) and VoiceOver (macOS and iOS) to check announcements, landmark navigation and live region updates. Colour contrast meets or exceeds WCAG AA ratios (4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text), and colour is never the only thing carrying information. For people who prefer reduced motion, the prefers-reduced-motion media query switches animation off.
accessibility.p3: Forms are built for clarity and error recovery. Labels are associated with their inputs, validation errors are announced to screen readers and linked with aria-describedby, and error messages say how to fix the problem. There is a legal side too: the Equality Act 2010 applies to businesses providing services to the public, and public sector bodies must meet the Public Sector Bodies (Websites and Mobile Applications) Accessibility Regulations 2018. Commercially, more people can use the site, everyone finds it easier, and search engines reward well-structured markup.
accessibility.p4: WCAG 2.2, published in October 2023, adds nine success criteria on top of WCAG 2.1 rather than replacing it, so a site that meets 2.2 Level AA also meets 2.1 Level AA. The additions mostly concern focus visibility and appearance, dragging alternatives, target size (a minimum 24 by 24 CSS pixels for interactive controls), consistent help placement, and reducing the cognitive load of authentication and redundant data entry. If a contract or tender asks you to meet "WCAG 2.1 AA", building to 2.2 satisfies it with room to spare.

gdpr.heading: UK GDPR and Data Protection
gdpr.subtitle: Privacy-first design and compliance with UK data protection law.
gdpr.p1: Every project is designed for UK GDPR compliance from the outset. Personal data processing rests on a lawful basis (consent, contractual necessity, legitimate interests, legal obligation), documented clearly in the privacy policy. Data minimisation means collecting only what is necessary. Purpose limitation keeps that data to the stated purpose, and storage limitation sets the retention period after which it is securely deleted. Consent for analytics and marketing cookies is obtained explicitly through opt-in banners under PECR (Privacy and Electronic Communications Regulations), and a user can withdraw that consent at any time, which triggers immediate deletion of tracking cookies.
gdpr.p2: Analytics are configured with privacy in mind. Google Analytics 4 runs with IP anonymisation, sensitive data is kept out of event parameters, and retention periods are set appropriately. Where a privacy-focused alternative suits the project better, I will recommend it. Data subject rights under UK GDPR (subject access requests, rectification, erasure, data portability and objection) are supported by clear processes and the technical work to back them. The ICO publishes the regulatory guidance, and I help clients work out what it means for them as data controllers.
gdpr.p3: Data in transit is encrypted using TLS 1.2 or higher (HTTPS everywhere), and sensitive data at rest is encrypted using industry-standard algorithms (AES-256). Where data is hosted, I prefer UK or EU data residency to avoid the complications of international transfers, which is straightforward on Microsoft Azure using the UK South or UK West regions. Backups are encrypted and tested regularly, and disaster recovery procedures are written against defined recovery time objectives (RTO) and recovery point objectives (RPO).
gdpr.disclaimer: This information is provided for general guidance and does not constitute legal advice. Consult a qualified data protection solicitor for specific legal requirements.

cloud.heading: Cloud-First Hosting
cloud.subtitle: Microsoft Azure and edge-optimised infrastructure.
cloud.p1: Hosting is cloud-first. Microsoft Azure provides scalable infrastructure with global edge delivery through Azure Static Web Apps, Azure App Service and Azure CDN. Static sites are deployed to the edge network and served from the location closest to each visitor, which keeps load times down. HTTPS is on by default, with certificates renewed automatically through Let's Encrypt or Azure-managed certificates.
cloud.p2: Development, staging and production environments are kept separate using Azure resource groups and deployment slots, so changes are tested before they reach the live site. Auto-scaling absorbs traffic spikes. Uptime is monitored with Azure Monitor and Application Insights, with alerts for slow responses, errors or downtime. Costs are kept in check through resource tagging, budget alerts and right-sized compute and storage. For a small business with predictable traffic, cloud hosting can be inexpensive.
cloud.p3: Infrastructure as code is used where the project needs it, defining resources in Bicep or Terraform so deployments are reproducible and changes are version-controlled. Backups run automatically and restores are tested, with rollback in place if a problem appears after release. Azure's UK regions (UK South, UK West) keep data inside the UK, which simplifies GDPR compliance and meets data residency requirements.

containers.heading: Containerisation and CI/CD
containers.subtitle: Docker and automated pipelines for reliable deployments.
containers.p1: Docker packages an application and its dependencies into an image that runs the same way in development, staging and production. Multi-stage builds discard everything the compile and test stages needed, so only the final runtime image is deployed. A smaller image means a smaller attack surface.
containers.p2: Images are pushed to a container registry (Azure Container Registry or Docker Hub) with version tags, so a failed deployment can be rolled back. Base images are kept up to date with security patches, and vulnerability scanners (Trivy, Snyk, Azure Defender) flag known CVEs in dependencies. Dependency installation is cached separately from application code, so builds skip downloads when nothing has changed.
containers.p3: CI/CD pipelines run each change through defined stages: lint checks for code style, type checks for TypeScript, unit and integration tests, an optimised build, and deployment to the target environment. Preview deployments let you review changes before anything is merged, and if a release introduces a bug, the pipeline can revert to the last working version quickly.

performance.heading: Performance and Core Web Vitals
performance.subtitle: Measured speed, because it affects search ranking and enquiries.
performance.p1: Performance is measured with Google's Core Web Vitals. Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) measures loading and should be under 2.5 seconds. Interaction to Next Paint (INP) measures responsiveness and should be under 200ms. Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) measures visual stability and should be under 0.1. These numbers affect user experience, conversion rates and Google rankings, so every project is built to meet the Good thresholds.
performance.p2: Images are served in modern formats (AVIF with WebP fallback) and sized for each screen with srcset and sizes. Offscreen images load as the visitor scrolls, which reduces the initial page weight. Fonts are self-hosted, subset to the characters needed and use font-display: swap so text is never invisible. Critical CSS is inlined so the top of the page renders immediately.
performance.p3: JavaScript is split by route, so visitors only download the code for the pages they open. Third-party scripts such as analytics load asynchronously so they do not block the page. Static assets are cached for a year with hashed filenames, so returning visitors load pages almost instantly.

seo.heading: Technical SEO
seo.subtitle: Search and answer-engine optimisation, built in from the start.
seo.p1: Technical SEO is what lets search engines crawl, index and rank your content. Semantic HTML structure with a correct heading hierarchy (one h1 per page, logical h2-h6 nesting) tells them what matters and how it relates. Metadata covers title tags (55-60 characters), meta descriptions (150-160 characters) and Open Graph tags for rich social media previews. JSON-LD structured data (Schema.org markup) adds explicit semantic context: LocalBusiness, Product, Article, BreadcrumbList and FAQPage schemas help search engines identify content types and show rich results in SERPs.
seo.p2: XML sitemaps list every page for crawlers, and robots.txt controls access to specific paths. Canonical URLs prevent duplicate content problems, and 301 redirects guide search engines when URLs change. Prerendering delivers complete HTML to crawlers on the first request, which is what makes JavaScript applications reliably indexable.
seo.p3: For businesses that serve more than one country or language, internationalisation (i18n) with hreflang tags signals the regional and language variants to search engines, which heads off duplicate content problems.

staticSites.heading: What a Static Site Is, and Why It Matters to You
staticSites.subtitle: The delivery model behind fast, cheap-to-run, hard-to-break websites.
staticSites.p1: A static site is one where every page is built into finished HTML when the site is published, instead of being assembled by a server on every visit. The browser receives a complete page straight away, with no database query and no rendering step to wait for.
staticSites.p2: For a business that means three things. It is fast, because the page is already made, which helps Core Web Vitals and search ranking. It is cheap to run, because serving files costs a fraction of running an application server. And it is hard to break into, with no database to compromise, no admin login exposed to the internet and no plugins to keep patched.
staticSites.p3: Anything dynamic (live stock levels, a customer account area, a booking calendar showing real availability) still needs a service behind it. So most of my builds are static pages with specific dynamic pieces added where needed. This website is built that way: every page is prerendered at build time.

builders.heading: Website Builders vs a Custom Build
builders.subtitle: How Wix, Squarespace, WordPress and a bespoke site compare.
builders.p1: Website builders do their job well. Wix plans run from around £9 to £119 a month and Squarespace from around £12 to £79 a month, both with templates, hosting and a visual editor included. If you need something online this week, are comfortable building it yourself, and the site is a simple shopfront, a builder is a reasonable choice.
builders.p2: The costs build up over time. Subscriptions continue for as long as the site exists and tend to rise. Templates limit what you can do, so the site looks like every other business on that template. Performance and accessibility are largely out of your hands, and both affect search ranking. Apps and add-ons are billed separately, often £5 to £30 a month each. And the site cannot move: a Wix site cannot be taken to another host.
builders.p3: WordPress sits in between. It is flexible and portable, but it is an application that needs maintaining. Core, theme and plugin updates have to be applied, and out-of-date plugins are the most common way into a small business website. Either you do that work every month or you pay somebody to.
builders.p4: A custom build starts from £100 and takes a little longer. You get a site designed for your business, built to accessibility and performance standards you can check, with no subscription attached to the site itself. For a business where the website brings in work, that usually pays for itself. If you only need a placeholder online by Friday, a builder is the better fit.

lifecycle.heading: The Delivery Lifecycle
lifecycle.subtitle: Five stages from first contact to launch and handover. Most small business sites run 2 to 6 weeks end to end.

stage1.title: Request and Discovery (1 to 2 days)
stage1.description: First contact is a no-obligation conversation by email or phone about what your business needs. I ask about your customers, what success looks like, existing systems and constraints, budget and deadlines. The aim is to understand the problem well enough to propose the right solution.
stage1.output1: Written summary of what was discussed

stage2.title: Proposal (2 to 3 days)
stage2.description: A written proposal sets out scope, the recommended approach and technology with reasons, and any assumptions and exclusions. For larger builds, phasing options let you start small and expand later. The proposal includes a fixed cost and a milestone plan showing what gets delivered and when. Starting prices are on the pricing page, so the figure should match what you expected.
stage2.output1: Proposal document with scope and approach
stage2.output3: Clear statement of what is and is not included

stage3.title: Refining Requirements (2 to 5 days)
stage3.description: Once the proposal is agreed, I turn it into a build plan: user stories with acceptance criteria, wireframes or clickable prototypes for key screens, data models and integration points, and requirements for accessibility, performance, security and GDPR. Everything is prioritised in a backlog so scope can change without derailing the project.
stage3.output1: Agreed backlog of user stories with acceptance criteria
stage3.output2: Wireframes or prototypes for key screens
stage3.output3: Technical design notes covering data and integrations

stage4.title: Build in Milestones (1 to 3 weeks)
stage4.description: Development is split into short iterations, each ending in a working version you can click through on a staging link. Each milestone comes with a written progress note covering what changed, what is next and spend against the plan, and we can discuss it by email or phone. If you request a change, you see its effect on cost and timeline before anything is agreed. Every change runs through lint, type checks, tests and accessibility checks automatically.
stage4.output1: Working software each milestone on a staging environment
stage4.output2: Written progress notes with staging links

stage5.title: Launch, Handover and Support (2 to 4 days)
stage5.description: Launch follows a checklist: accessibility audit, performance pass, security review, analytics and consent, SEO metadata and backups. Deployment has a rollback plan. Handover includes documentation, a walkthrough and transfer of the source code and infrastructure accounts. Ongoing support is optional.
stage5.output1: Live site or application on production infrastructure
stage5.output3: Source code and infrastructure ownership transferred

ai.heading: AI-Assisted and Agentic Delivery
ai.subtitle: Modern tooling, so more of the budget goes on design and testing.

item1.title: AI Tooling Throughout
item1.description: AI-assisted coding tools help with scaffolding, boilerplate, tests, refactoring, documentation and code review. That speeds up repetitive work while the quality checks stay the same.

item2.title: Agentic Workflows
item2.description: Agentic workflows handle multi-step tasks such as schema migrations, bulk refactors and generating TypeScript types from API specs. Work that used to take billable hours is automated, leaving more budget for design decisions and testing.

item3.title: More Budget for the Work That Matters
item3.description: More of your budget goes into requirements, user experience and testing, and less into boilerplate that tooling can produce faster.

item4.title: Human Accountability and Review
item4.description: Every line of code is reviewed by a person before it ships. Nothing is merged without passing automated checks (linting, type checking, tests, accessibility scans) and a manual review. Whatever tool produced the first draft, the developer is accountable for the result.

item5.title: Data Privacy and Guardrails
item5.description: AI tools have no access to client production data, secrets, API keys or sensitive business logic. Confidentiality and GDPR obligations decide what can be shared with third-party services, and if your project has strict data handling requirements, AI tooling is restricted or switched off.

quality.heading: Quality Gates
quality.subtitle: Seven checks every project passes before it goes live.

item1.title: Code Review
item1.description: Every change is reviewed before merge for code quality, correctness, test coverage and security.

item2.title: Automated Tests
item2.description: Unit tests cover individual functions and components, and end-to-end tests walk through the main user journeys. Tests run on every commit.

item3.title: Type Checking
item3.description: TypeScript catches type errors, null references and interface mismatches at compile time.

item4.title: Accessibility Checks
item4.description: Automated scans check for WCAG 2.2 Level AA issues such as missing alt text, low contrast, keyboard traps and unlabelled form fields, and manual screen reader testing confirms the site is usable.

item5.title: Performance Budgets
item5.description: Core Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS) are measured on every build, with budgets for bundle size, image weight and request count, so slowdowns are caught before launch.

item6.title: Dependency Scanning
item6.description: Automated scanning checks dependencies for known vulnerabilities. Security updates are applied promptly and tested before deployment.

item7.title: Staging Sign-Off
item7.description: Nothing goes live until you have reviewed and approved it on the staging site.

hosting.heading: Hosting and Environments
hosting.subtitle: Cloud-first infrastructure with automated deployments and rollback.
hosting.p1: Hosting is on Microsoft Azure, with separate development, staging and production environments. Docker builds keep them consistent, so what works in development works in production. Infrastructure as code (Bicep or Terraform) makes deployments reproducible and version-controlled.
hosting.p2: CI/CD pipelines lint, type-check and test the code automatically, build optimised bundles, and deploy to staging for review before production. If a release introduces a problem, the previous version can be restored within minutes.
hosting.p3: Monitoring tracks uptime, error rates and performance, with alerts for downtime, slow responses or spikes in errors. Backups run daily with retention policies, and restores are tested.

working.heading: Working Together
working.subtitle: What you can expect from me, and what I need from you.
working.p1: I am UK-based and work UK business hours (Monday to Friday, 9am to 5pm). You have one point of contact, the person building the site. We agree a channel that suits you (email, phone, Slack or Teams) and how often you want updates. Updates are written in plain language, and I will tell you when something turns out harder or simpler than expected.
working.p2: Your code, domain and hosting accounts are in your name from day one. There are no lock-in clauses or proprietary platforms, and no ongoing fees beyond standard hosting and domain costs. If you move the project in-house or to another developer, everything transfers with documentation and support during handover.
working.p3: Deadlines are agreed on what is achievable, and I will flag it when priorities conflict. Holidays and illness are flagged in advance, with a plan for anything urgent. When requirements change, I work out the effect on cost and timeline before starting new work, and if a deadline or budget looks at risk, you hear about it as soon as I know.

faq.heading: Common Questions
faq.subtitle: The questions I get asked most about how projects run.

q1.question: What if my requirements change mid-project?
q1.answer: Requirements change on most projects. At each milestone I can re-prioritise the backlog or adjust scope. If a change is significant, I work out the effect on cost and timeline and present options before going ahead.

q2.question: How can I see progress for myself?
q2.answer: Every milestone delivers a working version on a staging link that you can click through and test. Progress notes link to it and describe what was built, what changed and what comes next.

q3.question: Can we start small and expand later?
q3.answer: Yes. For larger projects, I propose phases where the first delivers a working first version or a specific set of high-value features. You launch with something useful, then expand as budget allows and priorities become clearer. It reduces risk and gets early feedback from your users.

q4.question: Who owns the code and the accounts?
q4.answer: You do. Source code is stored in a Git repository you own (GitHub, GitLab or Azure Repos). Hosting accounts, domain registrations and third-party accounts such as analytics and payment gateways are created in your name or transferred to you at handover.

q5.question: What happens after launch?
q5.answer: Support after launch is optional. I offer maintenance covering bug fixes, dependency updates, content changes and small new features. Or you can handle maintenance yourself or use another developer: the code is documented and there is a handover session so whoever takes it on can pick it up.

q6.question: How is AI used, and is my data safe?
q6.answer: AI tools help with scaffolding, boilerplate, refactoring, test generation and documentation. Every line is reviewed by a person and tested before it ships. AI tools have no access to production data, secrets, API keys or sensitive client information, and if your project has strict data handling requirements, they are restricted or switched off.

q7.question: How long does it take to build a small business website?
q7.answer: Most small business sites launch 2 to 6 weeks after first contact: 1 to 2 days of discovery, 2 to 3 days for the proposal, 2 to 5 days refining requirements, 1 to 3 weeks of build in weekly milestones, and 2 to 4 days for launch and handover. The biggest variable is how quickly the content arrives: photos, service descriptions and opening hours. That is where most projects stall.

q8.question: Should I use a small studio or a large agency?
q8.answer: A large agency has designers, copywriters, project managers and developers under one roof, which matters on a big multi-team build. You pay for that structure, and you usually deal with an account manager. A one-person studio gives you a direct line to the developer, lower overheads in the quote and faster decisions. For a small business website, an online shop or a booking system, that is usually the better fit.

item3.title: Being Found

cost.subtitle: What being hard to find online costs a business.
cost.p1: Enquiries go to a competitor who is easier to find. Customers shortlist businesses they can verify online before picking up the phone. If you do not have a website, you are not on that shortlist.
cost.p2: Being passed over can look like a quiet spell or a seasonal dip. Often it is because customers could not find you. Work goes to businesses that present better online, even when your work is better, and the same questions keep taking up your day when a page could answer them once.
cost.p3: Small business websites start at £100, and sites with online booking or payments start at £400. All starting prices, including the optional care plan, are on the pricing page.

howWorks.heading: How It Works
howWorks.subtitle: Four steps from first message to a live site.
howWorks.step1: A short conversation by email or phone about your business, what you offer, who your customers are, and what you want the site to do. No obligation.
howWorks.step2: A fixed written quote covering what is included, what is not, and a realistic timeframe. You decide whether to go ahead.
howWorks.step3: You send over your logo, photos and words. If you need help writing the content, guidance and templates are provided. Most small business sites need 500 to 1,000 words across all pages.
howWorks.step4: The site is built and you review it on a preview link. Changes are made from your feedback. Once you are happy, it goes live and you get a walkthrough of the contact form, updating content and checking analytics.
howWorks.fullProcess: Want to see the full delivery process in detail?

faq.heading: Common Questions
faq.subtitle: What small business owners ask before getting started.

q1.question: I'm not technical. Will I be able to manage it?
q1.answer: Yes. The site runs without you needing to touch code, and contact form submissions come to your email. If you want to edit text or add photos yourself, a simple content editor can be included, or you can send changes to me for a small fee. A walkthrough at handover shows you everything.

q2.question: Do I need to write all the content myself?
q2.answer: The core content (what you do, the areas you cover, your prices or approach) needs to come from you, because you know the business best. Templates and example text are provided to make that easier, and if you get stuck, a content session can turn a conversation into clear web copy.

q3.question: What if I already have a domain or a half-finished site?
q3.answer: Existing domains can be transferred or pointed at the new site without losing your email. A half-finished site can be replaced or, if the foundations are sound, completed. Every situation is different, so we go through it at the start.

q4.question: Will it work on phones?
q4.answer: Yes. Every site is designed mobile-first, which means it is built for phones and tablets before desktops. Most visitors to a small business site are on a phone, so that is where the design starts.

q5.question: Do I need a cookie banner and privacy policy?
q5.answer: Yes, if you use analytics or any tracking. UK GDPR and PECR require consent before setting non-essential cookies, and you must tell visitors what data you collect and why. A compliant cookie banner and privacy policy are included as standard and linked in the footer.

q6.question: Can it grow later if my business grows?
q6.answer: Yes. Sites are built with maintainable code on modern infrastructure, so adding booking, an online shop, a blog or extra service pages later is straightforward.

q7.question: What happens if I want changes after it's live?
q7.answer: Minor fixes in the first month are included. After that, small changes such as text updates, new photos or an extra page are handled pay-as-you-go or through the optional care plan.

ecommerce.subtitle: An online shop with secure payments, stock control and no monthly platform fee attached to the site itself.

intro.p1: I build online shops for independent retailers across the UK, from a single-product store to a full catalogue with variants, stock levels and delivery zones. Payments run through Stripe or PayPal, so card data never touches your site and you are not liable for storing it.
intro.p2: The main difference from a hosted platform is ownership. A Shopify or Wix shop runs on a subscription that continues for as long as you trade, apps are billed separately, and the shop cannot move elsewhere. A custom shop has its code, domain and hosting account in your name, with no compulsory monthly fee for the site itself.
intro.p3: That is not right for everyone. If you are selling a handful of items and want to be live this week, a hosted platform is the better choice. Custom pays back when the shop is a major sales channel, when it needs its own look, or when it has to connect to the stock and accounting systems you already use.

pricing.body: Online shops are quoted individually, because a ten-product shop and a two-hundred-product shop are different jobs. You get a fixed written quote before any work starts.

faq.heading: Questions About Online Shops
faq.subtitle: What retailers ask me before committing.

q1.question: Is a custom shop cheaper than Shopify or Wix in the long run?
q1.answer: It depends how long you trade and how many add-ons you need. A hosted platform costs roughly £20 to £100 a month once apps are included, for as long as you trade. A custom shop costs more to build and then only hosting, which for a static-fronted shop is a few pounds a month. Most shops break even within two to four years. For a short-term or seasonal shop, a hosted platform makes more sense.

q2.question: Can I manage products myself without touching code?
q2.answer: Yes. You get an admin area for adding and editing products, prices, stock levels and images. If your catalogue already lives in a spreadsheet, an EPOS system or an accounting package, I can often import from it or sync with it.

q3.question: How are card payments kept secure?
q3.answer: Card details are entered directly into Stripe or PayPal's own hosted checkout, so they never pass through or get stored on your site. That keeps you out of scope for the strictest parts of PCI DSS compliance. Your site only ever sees whether a payment succeeded and what was ordered.

q4.question: Will my products show up in Google Shopping?
q4.answer: Every product gets Product structured data: price, availability, images and description. That is what Google reads to build a shopping result. It makes products eligible, though Google decides placement, and paid Shopping campaigns are a separate service I do not run.

q5.question: What about postage, VAT and returns?
q5.answer: Postage rules, delivery zones and collection options are set up as part of the build, so a customer nearby and a customer in Inverness can be charged differently. VAT is handled correctly on invoices. Returns policy wording is yours to decide, but I will make sure it is published where UK consumer law requires it to be.

booking.title: Stop Losing Bookings to Voicemail
booking.subtitle: Let customers book themselves in at any hour, without you answering the phone mid-appointment.

intro.p1: Most missed bookings are lost because somebody rang while you were busy, did not leave a message, and booked with whoever answered next. An online booking system takes that booking for you at eleven at night, on a Sunday, or while you are with a client.
intro.p2: Booking is built into your own website, so customers stay on your site with your prices, photos and reviews in front of them, and the booking comes to you directly instead of through a platform that also advertises your competitors.
intro.p3: If you already use Booksy, Square or something similar and it works, I integrate with it. Your site becomes the front door and the existing system stays the diary. If you have no system, or yours does not fit how you work, I build one that does.

included.heading: What a Booking System Includes
included.subtitle: The parts that stop double-bookings and no-shows.
included.f1: Live availability from your own calendar
included.f2: Service and duration selection, so a cut and a colour book different slots
included.f3: Staff or resource assignment, where more than one person takes bookings
included.f4: Confirmation and reminder emails, which is what brings no-shows down
included.f5: Deposits or full payment at booking through Stripe, if you want them
included.f6: Cancellation and rescheduling rules you set, enforced automatically
included.f7: Booksy, Square, Google Calendar or Outlook integration where you already use one
included.f8: Buffer times, opening hours and holiday blocks that respect how you work

whoFor.heading: Who It Suits
whoFor.subtitle: The businesses that get the most out of online booking.
whoFor.item1Description: Hairdressers, barbers and beauty salons where a full diary is the whole business and every unanswered call is a lost slot.
whoFor.item2Description: Physios, dentists, podiatrists, counsellors and therapists who need appointment types of different lengths and sensible cancellation rules.
whoFor.item3Description: Electricians, plumbers and surveyors booking quote visits, where travel time between jobs has to be built into the slot.
whoFor.item4Description: Fitness instructors, tutors and workshop hosts selling places in a session rather than one-to-one appointments, with capacity limits and waiting lists.

pricing.heading: What a Booking System Costs
pricing.body: A website with booking or payment integration starts at £400 and typically takes 2 to 3 weeks to build. That covers a working booking flow connected to your calendar, with confirmations and reminders. More complex setups (multiple staff, deposits, class capacity, syncing with an existing system) are quoted in writing before work starts.

faq.heading: Questions About Booking Systems
faq.subtitle: What salons and trades ask me before committing.

q1.question: I already use Booksy. Do I have to move?
q1.answer: No. If Booksy works for you, keep it. I integrate with it so your website shows live availability and passes the booking across. Moving only makes sense if you have outgrown it, or if its own marketing is pointing your customers at competitors.

q2.question: Will it stop people booking when I'm closed or already busy?
q2.answer: Yes. Availability comes from your calendar, with opening hours, buffer times, holidays and existing appointments all taken into account, so double-bookings cannot happen.

q3.question: Can I take a deposit to cut down no-shows?
q3.answer: Yes, through Stripe: either a fixed deposit or the full amount at the point of booking, and you choose which services require it. Together with automatic reminder emails, deposits are the most effective way to reduce no-shows. You set the cancellation and refund terms, and the system applies them.

q4.question: What happens if a customer wants to change or cancel?
q4.answer: Their confirmation email includes a link to reschedule or cancel within the window you set, for example more than 24 hours ahead. Outside that window it asks them to contact you instead.

q5.question: Do I need a whole new website to get booking?
q5.answer: Not always. Booking can often be added to an existing site if it is in reasonable shape and you control it. If the site is on a platform you cannot modify, or is slow and hard to find in search, rebuilding usually gets you more. The booking work is the same either way.

businessWebsite.title: A Website That Does the Explaining For You
businessWebsite.subtitle: For businesses that do not sell online or take bookings, and need to be found and trusted.

intro.p1: Plenty of businesses do not need a shop or a booking diary. They need a site that appears when somebody searches, answers the questions asked on every first call, and looks like it belongs to a firm worth hiring. It is a smaller job than an online shop and costs less.
intro.p2: Most of the work is structure and clarity. Each service gets its own page so it can rank for what people search: a roofer needs separate pages for flat roofs, repairs and emergency callouts. Contact details are on every page, with enough detail that prospects can decide whether you are right for them before they get in touch.
intro.p3: If somebody is about to hand you a significant job, they will look you up first. A site that loads quickly, reads well and works on a phone helps at that moment. A slow, dated site works against you.

included.heading: What a Business Website Includes
included.subtitle: The structure that makes a site findable and credible.
included.f1: A dedicated page per service, so each can rank for its own search
included.f2: Service-area content for the places you cover
included.f3: Contact details and a working enquiry form reachable from every page
included.f4: Photo galleries of finished work, optimised so they do not slow the site
included.f5: LocalBusiness structured data feeding Google's local results for the areas you serve
included.f6: WCAG 2.2 Level AA accessibility and Core Web Vitals performance targets
included.f7: Cookie banner and privacy policy meeting UK GDPR and PECR
included.f8: Content you can update yourself: hours, prices, a new service

whoFor.heading: Who It Suits
whoFor.subtitle: Businesses that need a website to win trust and enquiries.
whoFor.item1Description: Accountants, solicitors, surveyors and independent consultants, where the site has to hold up when a prospective client checks you out.
whoFor.item2Description: Builders, roofers and electricians who miss search traffic by listing every service on one page instead of giving each its own.
whoFor.item3Description: Businesses whose site was fine a decade ago and is now slow, hard to read on a phone, and losing enquiries as a result.
whoFor.item4Description: Charities, clubs and community organisations that need clear, accessible public information on a modest budget.

pricing.heading: What a Business Website Costs
pricing.body: A business website starts at £100 for up to five pages, with typically 1 to 2 weeks of build time once I have your content. More pages, extra service pages, or content that needs writing will add to that, and you get the exact figure in a written quote before anything starts.

faq.heading: Questions About Business Websites
faq.subtitle: What firms ask me before committing.

q1.question: How many pages do I need?
q1.answer: Usually one for each thing you want to be found for, plus the basics. A plumber offering boiler repairs, bathroom installation and emergency callouts needs three service pages. Five pages covers most small firms, and ten is common once every service has its own.

q2.question: Do I have to write all the content myself?
q2.answer: No, though supplying the raw material speeds things up and keeps the cost down. Most small business sites need 500 to 1,000 words in total. Send rough notes, a list of services and some photos and I can shape it from there. Writing it from scratch is quoted as extra.

q3.question: What if I already have a domain or a half-finished site?
q3.answer: That is common and usually fine. An existing domain can be moved across without downtime, and a half-finished site is often useful for its content and photos even if the build is not worth keeping.

q4.question: Can it grow later if the business grows?
q4.answer: Yes. Adding pages, a blog, booking or a shop later is normal. The site is built on standard technology, so expanding it does not mean starting again, and any developer can work on it.

q5.question: Will it work on phones?
q5.answer: Yes, and that is where most of your visitors will be. Every site is designed mobile-first and built to pass Google's Core Web Vitals thresholds, which measure loading, responsiveness and visual stability on the devices people use.

bespoke.kicker: Bespoke software development / UK-wide, delivered remotely
bespoke.title: When Off-the-Shelf Software Nearly Fits
bespoke.subtitle: Client portals, internal tools, dashboards and workflow systems, built around the way your business runs.

intro.p1: Most businesses reach a point where the software shapes the process instead of serving it. The signs are familiar: a spreadsheet nobody dares edit, the same information typed into three systems, a monthly report that takes two days, or a subscription paid for one feature out of forty.
intro.p2: I design and build custom web applications for that gap: client portals, booking and scheduling systems, internal dashboards, quoting tools, and integrations that make existing systems talk to each other. Built on .NET or Node with a typed front end, hosted on Microsoft Azure, with the same accessibility and security standards as everything else I ship.
intro.p3: Sometimes buying is the better option. If a £30-a-month product does ninety per cent of what you need, I will recommend it. Custom software is worth it when the remaining ten per cent is where your margin lives, when nothing off the shelf fits the workflow, or when licence costs across your team have grown past the cost of owning the software.

included.f6: Authentication, role-based permissions and audit trails where needed
included.f7: Automated tests, type checking and CI so it survives future changes

whoFor.heading: Who It Suits
whoFor.subtitle: The problems where building beats buying.
whoFor.item1Description: Firms whose clients need somewhere to see their own documents, jobs, invoices or progress without emailing to ask.
whoFor.item2Description: Businesses that depend on a fragile spreadsheet, where one wrong paste can cost a week.
whoFor.item3Description: Organisations retyping the same data into a booking system, an accounts package and a CRM because none of them talk to each other.
whoFor.item4Description: Businesses whose software is the product, needing a technical partner to build or extend it to a high standard.

pricing.heading: What Bespoke Software Costs
pricing.body: Bespoke work is quoted individually because scope varies more than in any other kind of project: the same short description can mean two weeks or six months. You start with a free discovery conversation by email or phone, a clear view on whether building is the right call, and a fixed written quote with its assumptions and exclusions before any work begins.

faq.heading: Questions About Bespoke Software
faq.subtitle: What businesses ask before commissioning a build.

q1.question: How do I know custom is the right answer?
q1.answer: Often it is not, and I will say so. Buy off the shelf when a product covers the need at a sensible licence cost. Build when nothing fits the workflow, when workarounds cost hours every week, when data has to move between systems that cannot connect, or when per-seat licensing for a growing team has passed what owning the software would cost. Discovery answers that question before you spend anything.

q2.question: Can we start small instead of committing to everything?
q2.answer: Yes, and for most projects I recommend it. The first phase delivers a useful part of the system (one workflow or one user group) that your team can start using. How they use it usually shapes phase two, and learning that early costs far less than building everything first.

q3.question: What happens if we want to take it elsewhere?
q3.answer: Everything transfers. Source code lives in a repository you own from day one, hosting and third-party accounts are in your name, and handover includes documentation and a walkthrough.

q4.question: Is AI used in the build, and is our data safe?
q4.answer: AI tools help with scaffolding, boilerplate, refactoring, test generation and documentation, and every line is reviewed by a person and tested before it ships. AI tools are not given access to production data, secrets, API keys or client information. If your project has specific data handling requirements, they go into the written scope at discovery.

q5.question: What about support after launch?
q5.answer: Support is optional. It can be a maintenance arrangement covering fixes, dependency updates and small changes, or a handover to your own team or another developer. The code is documented either way.

intercopy.title: InterCopy
intercopy.summary: A translation management platform for teams shipping products in several languages.
intercopy.description: InterCopy is a translation management platform for teams shipping products in several languages. It replaces the usual spreadsheets and chat threads with a shared workspace: a content tree for organising strings, a side-by-side translation grid, a review workflow with sign-off history, and a glossary and style-rule engine that catches inconsistent terminology before it ships. A Figma plugin syncs designs to the content behind them, so translators can see the screen a string appears on. Locale files export to i18next, vue-i18n, react-intl and next-intl, and an API and CI/CD integration send translations straight into a build pipeline. Built end to end with an ASP.NET Core 10 API, PostgreSQL, Keycloak for authentication, a Nuxt 4 front end and a TypeScript Figma plugin, deployed on dedicated infrastructure with GitHub Actions for CI/CD.
features: Content tree and multi-language translation grid
Review workflow with verdicts and full history
Figma plugin with live sync between designs and translated content
Glossary and style-rule enforcement for consistent terminology
API and CI/CD integration for automated locale exports
